newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australia wages data a sign rates are on hold.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australia wages data a sign rates are on hold.

text.p: Further evidence that the pace of Australian wages growth is moderating showed interest rates are likely to remain on hold and inflation stay moderate, but there are some risks further ahead in 1997, economists said.

Department of Industrial Relations (DIR) figures showed on Wednesday that the average annualised wage increase (AAWI) for all federal wage agreements in the December quarter was 4.4 percent, down from 4.8 percent in the September quarter.
Private sector agreements in the December quarter showed an AAWI of 4.4 percent, down from 5.3 percent in the third quarter.
"To me this is quite an encouraging sign that wage growth is coming back, certainly into areas where the Reserve Bank will be less worried," Commonwealth Bank chief economist Bruce Freeland said.

While the RBA would not relax or become complacent about wages, Freeland said the data was "just a sign at this stage that wages pressures look to be under control, certainly look to be very consistent with continuing 2-3 percent core inflation."
Economists said the numbers covered about 20 percent of the nation's workforce, and while the inflation outlook was positive, there were still threats on the wages front.

The RBA has previously said that all-up wages growth of 4.5 percent was its "line in the sand" on wages growth, above which it would start to threaten the RBA's two to three percent underlying inflation target.
"Today's numbers may provide the RBA with some encouragement that wages secured under bargaining agreements are under control," Hambros fixed income economist Su-Lin Ong said.
"However, there are uncertainties on the wages front and upside risk to wages growth in the longer term," she said.

And that outlook meant that rates were likely to be on hold for the time being, and definitely until the result of the Australian Council of Trade Union's (ACTU) "living wage" claim, expected in March, was known.
It also meant that any hopes of a near term rate cut on the back of the data were overly optimistic, analysts said.
"That battle was lost a few weeks ago," Colonial State Bank chief economist Hans Kunnen said.
"With rate cuts behind us and solid global economic growth, Australian interest rates are on hold," he said.
Apart from the union wage claim, the prospect of stronger economic growth in 1996 also suggested that wages could strengthen later in the year.

"Continued uncertainties over the ACTU "living wage" claim and the likely pick-up in overall wages as the economy gathers strength through 1997 suggests that the wages risks remain in the upside," Societe Generale economist Glenn Maguire said.
Economists receive a further update on wages on Thursday, when final data on average weekly ordinary time earnings (AWOTE) for the three months to November are released.
Preliminary data released earlier this month showed AWOTE rose 1.2 percent in the quarter and 3.9 percent over the year.

This was at the top end of expectations, but economists said it may have been boosted by special factors in the public sector, which may become more apparent in Thursday's data which provides a breakdown between public and private sector wages.

One of these factors is that recent public sector cutbacks may have mainly affected low income earners, and as they drop out of the calculations of AWOTE, there is an upward shift in reported AWOTE, even though pay rises of that magnitude are not being given, analysts said. -- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373 1800
